newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ fiscal position must back monetary policy-Birch.
newsitem.headline: NZ fiscal position must back monetary policy-Birch.

text.p: Planned extra spending by the new Coalition Government had to take account of the need to support monetary policy in maintaining price stability, New Zealand Finance Minister Bill Birch said on Tuesday.

Asked by reporters at the National Party Conference if the government would spend less in 1997/98 than the $1.2 billion extra spending identified in the coalition agreement, he said: "The limits have been set having regard to the pressure on monetary policy.
"We need to have a fiscal positon that is supportive of monetary policy so treasury ministers will take all these things into account."

Commenting on Treasurer Winston Peters' requests for departments to outline potential spending cuts for next year by today, Birch said the government had got "indicative implementation plans" from ministers in big spending portfolios about possible cuts.
"They are an instrument to assess the size of our problem and the opportunities for savings."
He said there was a long way to go and this was just one step in the budget process.
Birch was speaking after the party had been addressed by Manufacturers Federation chief executive Simon Arnold.
Arnold said New Zealand's standard of living lagged Australia and urged New Zealand to continue the reform process.
"We wanted to see world class intervention in the economy to ensure that the economy will continue to grow and grow faster than the Australian economy," he told reporters.
He repeated comments that a $100 million injection of extra spending earmarked for business was unneeded.
"We did make passing reference to that. It's on the table.
"We re-expressed the issue about the fiscal position and the problem spending this year is going to create for us in terms of the dollar."
He said they spent most time talking about building a more competitive and faster growing economy and urged the government to "get back on their bike".
"We are concerned the economic costs of proposals are not given enough attention in the process of policy making."
The way government intervenes was not given enough attention.
He said the $100 million business allocation was a low priority and could be foregone.
Birch said the $100 million was part of the Coalition Agreement and it was for the government to set priorities.
"It is part of the Coalition Agreement and there is a commitment to it."
He said he would not make judgements on whether it was low priority on its merits.
"As we now look at the reality of the Coalition Agreement there are fiscal parameters not only for this budget... but right up to 1999/00.
"We have to carefully cost these commitments now in a way that we weren't able to do during the negotiations.
"The negotiations were taken under a fair bit of necessity to get them concluded and some of these things need to be costed very carefully," Birch said.
